News.title: Dickens' classic gets modern slang spin to help parents keep up
News.content:
Dickens' classic gets modern slang spin to help parents keep up

Charles Dickens' timeless novel Great Expectations has been reimagined as Bare Expectations - a Gen Alpha-friendly audiobook designed to help parents navigate today's teen slang.

MC Grindah teams up with Tesco Mobile to help parents understand their kids

Charles Dickens' classic novel 'Great Expectations' has been given a Gen Alpha makeover - reimagined in today's slang. Renamed 'Bare Expectations', the tale has been 'translated' into teen speak to help parents better understand the language their children use today.

‌



It comes after research of 2,000 parents with children aged between 10 and 16 found 70% have struggled to understand a text message, social media post or online comment written by their child because of slang.

‌



Commissioned by Tesco Mobile, it is available as an audiobook on Spotify and Apple Music . It has been paired with a glossary explaining some of the most misunderstood words and phrases to help parents make sense of modern digital language and encourage conversations about online safety.

‌



View 3 Images The reimaging tells the Charles Dickens’ classic through Gen Alpha slang (Image: PinPep)

To bring the adaptation to life, Tesco Mobile partnered with Kurupt FM's MC Grindah, who was invited to a youth centre in London to give a reading of 'Bare Expectations' to local parents and teens.

MC Grindah, who hopes the project helps families bridge generational language gaps, said, "You'd think the best MC in the galaxy would know all the latest slang, and I do.

‌



"If any kid tells you otherwise, they're lying. Any words I don't know are just not cool enough for me to care about."

The modern-day adaptation has been launched alongside the mobile network's new Safe Start offering – a guided phone-readiness experience, designed to help parents feel more confident that their child's phone is safely set up and ready for day one.

View 3 Images It aims to help parents better understand the language their children use today (Image: PinPep)

‌



The phone network also partnered with Chloe Combi, author, researcher, and one of the world's foremost experts on Generation Z and Generation A, to advise on the translation of the novel into modern teen slang and provide crucial insights into youth culture.

Chloe Combi said: "Teen slang is evolving at an unprecedented pace. A word can emerge as a social media craze one day and become everyday language the next.

"'Bare Expectations' funnily shows how much communication has evolved by translating a familiar story into today's youth language, helping parents understand their children's world and start more confident conversations."

‌



The study found 41% of parents whose children use slang look up a word, abbreviation or emoji at least once a week in an effort to keep up with the latest terminology.

The glossary and audiobook form part of the launch of Safe Start, which offers customisable parental controls, AI-powered social media monitoring through Sway.ly, and expert online safety resources to help families navigate the digital world with confidence.

‌



Laura Joseph, the mobile network's chief customer officer, said: "Parents don't need to speak their children's language to help keep them safe online, but they do need the confidence to start the conversation.

"With many parents telling us that teen slang and rapidly changing online trends can make it harder to spot potential issues, Safe Start is designed to help bridge that gap.

"By combining expert online safety guidance with AI-powered social media monitoring through Sway.ly, we're giving families practical tools to better understand the digital world young people are navigating every day and support safer online experiences."

‌



View 3 Images The modern version is available as an audiobook (Image: PinPep)

Nearly half (49%) of parents worry about inappropriate content being shared with their child, while 48% fear strangers making contact online, and 40% worry about bullying and exclusion.

And while parents said the hardest conversation they have with their kids relates to inappropriate content (27%), 84% chat to their child about staying safe online at least once a month, according to the survey by OnePoll.

Article continues below

Daniela Fernandez, co-founder of Sway.ly and who notes that parents want to protect their children online but often struggle to understand their digital world and language, said: "That's why we've partnered on this new Safe Start SIM. "Our technology gives parents insights into their children's social media use, alongside practical tools and guidance, so they can spot problems early and act with confidence.

"The 'Bare Expectations' campaign further helps families start important conversations for a healthier online experience."

News.title: Peppa Pig bush 'beheaded' by heartless vandals sparking police appeal
News.content:
Peppa Pig bush 'beheaded' by heartless vandals sparking police appeal

Police have put out an appeal to the public for information or dashcam footage after a hedge sculpture of Peppa Pig was found with its head cut off - the owner called the incident 'distressing'

View 4 Images The Peppa Pig shaped hedge has lost its head after vandals appeared to attack it with a saw (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

A beloved bush carefully sculpted into the shape of children's cartoon favourite Peppa Pig has been "beheaded" by cruel vandals as police launch a probe into the incident.

‌



The popular topiary, which took years to grow, was discovered with its head hacked off and the owners believe a saw was taken to their sculpture.

‌



Laura Hinton, whose family created and took care of the special 4ft hedge sculpture, said she has been left "devastated" by the senseless act.

‌



The Peppa Pig topiary had its head cut off between August 13 and 15 near the village of Newton Purcell, on the route towards Bicester, Oxfordshire. Laura's family said the damage across four separate stumps appeared to have been deliberate.

Peppa Pig hits back at Charli XCX as bizarre feud escalates READ MORE :

View 4 Images The Peppa Pig hedge before it was 'decapitated' (Image: / SWNS)

She said: "It has taken years to grow. This was distressing not only because of the nature of the vandalism but also the time, effort and dedication topiary takes.

‌



"Peppa was loved by the locals and by visitors alike. The head they cut off was not left at the scene. They must have taken it with them. They must have also brought their own saw.

View 4 Images The owner said 'Peppa was loved by the locals and visitors' (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

Laura shared her safety concerns following the shocking incident, adding that the act "also suggests a level of concern for personal safety, as someone was around the property with a saw".

‌



Thames Valley Police have put out an appeal for information and asked anyone with information to come forward. A spokesperson said: "We have received a report of criminal damage on Buckingham Road, Newton Purcell, as you have described below.

View 4 Images The topiary was finished off with red boots (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

"We would ask anyone with information, dash-cam or CCTV footage to contact the force on 101 or by making a report via our website quoting reference 43260423720."

Article continues below

Peppa Pig first appeared on Britain's TV screens more than 22 years ago in May 2004. The show's ninth series began broadcasting in summer last year.

The hugely popular show has sparked theme parks across Europe and the US and in 2024 the cartoon received its own store in Battersea Power Station, central London.

News.title: 'Doctors told me I was infertile - then I took a pregnancy test'
News.content:
'Doctors told me I was infertile - then I took a pregnancy test'

Shannon Maya Lamb was told she could not fall pregnant again after battling cancer while pregnant with her son, Hunter

View 6 Images Shannon and her first child (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

A mum who was diagnosed with ovarian cancer while pregnant with her first child and told chemotherapy would leave her infertile has just given birth to her second 'miracle' baby. Shannon Maya Lamb, 31, was diagnosed with aggressive ovarian cancer in October 2020, after spotting a lump on her pelvis while lying in the bath.

‌



She had invasive surgery to remove the tumour and discovered she was pregnant with her first child in March 2022. But the news came weeks after learning her ovarian cancer had already spread to her lung, and she needed surgery to remove a portion of it.

‌



When a CT scan revealed at 31 weeks pregnant that there was further disease in a 4cm lymph node beside her lung, she needed emergency chemotherapy and an emergency caesarean section to deliver her premature son, Hunter, who is now three.

‌



What followed were 11 further rounds of aggressive chemotherapy and two stem cell transplants. In October 2024, she was confirmed to be in remission - but due to the life-saving cancer treatments, she was told she could not fall pregnant again.

View 6 Images Shannon was diagnosed with ovarian cancer while pregnant with her first child (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

But in November 2025, she got sore breasts and a period - and discovered she had fallen pregnant again. Single mum Shannon, who is now over two years cancer free, was delighted to learn she was expecting a healthy baby girl, who was born last month.

‌



Biomedical science student Shannon, from Dundee, who spoke to Talk to the Press, said: "I remember first noticing this lump on the side of my pelvis, and my hair began to thin.

"I first questioned if it was a hernia but it ended up causing the worst pain I'd ever felt. It was aggressive cancer and I had surgery all alone because of Covid. But in early 2022 I got shortness of breath and I found out there was a 'suspicious' nodule in my lung, the same week I learned I was pregnant.

Dr Amir Khan shares 'end-of-the-bed' test GPs do on every patient READ MORE :

"I had surgery at 16 weeks pregnant, but the cancer had already spread. I had Hunter at 31 weeks and went down to the chemo unit four days later. I needed to say alive for my son, I'd have given up without him.

‌



"I was told I would be infertile after the stem cell transplants - I just had to accept it. So it's a miracle I'm here, my son is here, and I have my miracle baby daughter too."

Shannon was first diagnosed with germ cell ovarian cancer after spotting a lump on her abdomen, which grew within a matter of weeks. She said: "I had been lying in the bath. It was hard, and my friend suggested it might a hernia. I didn't know what was wrong."

She was referred to gynaecology and it was confirmed to be a 14cm by 13cm cancerous tumour on her left ovary. On December 22, she underwent surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary to remove the infected ovary and surrounding affected areas.

‌



From then, she was discharged and given regular scans as it was believed to have removed all the cancer. She was thrilled to learn she had fallen pregnant in April 2022.

However, around the same time, Shannon began suffering with shortness of breath, fatigue, aching joints and weight loss. A chest x-ray revealed a 'suspicious shadow' on her lung - which biopsies later revealed were a relapse.

View 6 Images Shannon was told chemo would leave her infertile (Image: SWNS)

‌



At 16 weeks, Shannon had a surgery to remove the bottom lobe of her right lung, which contained five tumours. But at 29 weeks pregnant, a CT scan revealed the cancer had already spread and there were tumours on her lymph node, spine, coccyx, left pelvic bone and by her kidney.

Shannon said: "I started chemotherapy at 31 weeks and gave birth to Hunter just after that. Four days after my emergency c-section I was back having more chemotherapy.

"I just wanted to be with my baby, but I couldn't. I had to FaceTime him with the nurses. When I could finally see him, it was only for 30 minutes a day when I was disconnected from the chemo, and I had to wear gloves."

‌



View 6 Images Shannon spotted a lump on her pelvis while lying in the bath (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

Shannon spent the following months having 11 rounds of chemotherapy, and then two stem cell transplants with high-dose chemo. Throughout the course of the stem cell transplants, Shannon caught sepsis twice, and feared at points she would not survive.

By August 2023, the treatment was over, and a surgery in October 2024 to remove bones in her spine to test for cancer revealed it was gone, and had been in remission since July 2023. She has now been in remission for three years.

‌



But she was warned before the chemotherapy and stem cell transplants that eradicating the cancer would cost her her fertility. Shannon said: "Especially with one ovary, I was told the chance of recovering ovary function was pretty much nil.

"I was deemed infertile and menopausal, and prescribed hormone replacement therapy (HRT). But in July 2025, I began questioning my fertility - I was still having period-like bleeds.

"I requested blood checks, which confirmed I was post-menopausal - and two pregnancy tests came back negative. I thought, 'this is stupid, I'm clearly infertile' but decided to do a digital test anyway. I was confident it would be negative - until it said, 'pregnant'."

‌



View 6 Images Shannon has just given birth to her second 'miracle' baby (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

Incredibly, Shannon was indeed expecting a baby girl – and miracle baby Zayla was born via c-section on July 22. Shannon had some complications and was hospitalised after her bowel became obstructed in the weeks leading up to the birth, and Zayla suffered with three bouts of jaundice shortly after birth.

But now the family are all happy, healthy and safe at home and Shannon is loving being a mum-of-two. She said: "During treatment, I was on death's door. I would never have imagined now I'd have a healthy little boy and a little girl.

‌



"I'm meant to be infertile! My friend joked I must just have a really strong ovary. I'm being monitored but as far as we are aware, I'm still completely cancer free.

View 6 Images Shannon and her second child (Image: Shannon Maya Lamb/SWNS)

"The whole thing has been miraculous - unbelievable and a blessing. I'm grateful to have been given a second chance at life, and my little girl is a miracle.

Article continues below

“I look at her and I’m so in love, I can’t find the words to describe it. I’m so blessed to have both my daughter and my son. I’m so, so lucky.

"I hope my story might give others hope - when there doesn't seem like there can be a happy ending, there might still be one anyway."

News.title: Harry and Meghan's security arrangements a private matter, PM says
News.content:
The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.

King Charles was told of the move on Sunday. There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.

The Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.

They were last in the UK in July to visit the King and Queen Camilla, in what was seen as a key development in their relationship.

The Palace described the meeting at the King's private home in Gloucestershire as a "private family occasion".

It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.

It is understood that July's visit had to be adjusted after the duke's request for police protection was rejected.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge in which he sought to overturn a decision that had downgraded his security after his move to the US.

At the time, he told the BBC that he "can't see a world" in which he would bring his family to the UK due to the downgrading of his protection.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

Royal expert Robert Hardman told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme it was likely that some of their past security issues "have been resolved" but details - or who is going to foot the bill - are still unknown.

The children's enrolment in school indicated a "clear direction of travel", Hardman said, adding that the children are now going to be raised as "British rather than American".

In the US, the Sussexes have employed a private security team to protect them.

They offered no comment when asked by the BBC whether that team would be moving to the UK with them.

News.title: Harry and Meghan are experts in surprise - but why are they returning to UK now?
News.content:
This has been a relatively sudden decision.

I've now spoken to people who know the couple well. Although there had been general discussions about the possibility of spending more time in the UK, the decision to move back was made recently.

The family's visit to the UK in July was significant.

As well as spending time with the King at Highgrove, Harry, Meghan and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are said to have loved being with the family of Harry's mother, Diana, Princess of Wales.

The children met their aunts, uncles and cousins. The visit to Europe, which included time in Portugal, where they have a home, was described to me as "such a great time" for the family. It turned a possible move back to the UK into a firm decision.

I am told that this move is not due to any problems in the US. It has been driven by the couple's desire to spend time in Europe, nearer Harry's family and wanting to educate their children in the UK.

Schools have been chosen for Archie and Lilibet. New terms for virtually all schools in England start by the second week of September. The Sussexes will need to settle in so we can expect the family to be back in the UK within the next 10 days.

News.title: Travelodge boss resigns as chain tackles security after sex assault at hotel
News.content:
The boss of Travelodge, Jo Boydell, has stepped down as the group addresses safety issues after a sexual assault at one of its hotels.

A woman staying at a hotel in Maidenhead was sexually assaulted in December 2022 after a man lied to staff to get a key card to her room. Kyran Smith was jailed for more than seven years for the attack.

Many people have since contacted the BBC over room security incidents at Travelodges and a review of security measures at the firm is under way.

Boydell had been criticised for the firm's handling of safety issues. She said she only heard about the assault years after it had happened, although it emerged the victim had emailed her shortly after the attack.

When questioned about the victim's email, sent in January 2023 one month after the assault, Boydell said it had been "handled on my behalf" and there had been "serious failures".

Earlier this month, a domestic violence victim told the BBC how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.

The woman said she was "failed" by the chain and described it as one of the "most traumatic nights of my life" after the man kicked the door off its hinges.

She said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."

Instead, she was offered another room in the hotel.

In another incident, a couple in Scotland woke to find a shirtless man in their hotel bedroom after he was mistakenly given a key card to their door.

In April, a group of hotel guests said they were given keys to other people's rooms twice in one week at a Travelodge branch in Newham, east London.

John Nowell, who was part of a corporate group staying at the hotel, told the BBC that his key card allowed him into a room where the occupant was in the middle of a shower.

Liberal Democrat Freddie van Mierlo is the MP for Thame, where Travelodge's HQ is based, and has previously called for Boydell to resign. On Thursday, he told the BBC he was pleased that she was leaving the firm.

"I've always said that what's wrong is the business model â it's made far too many cuts, deep cuts, to the company in order to have a low-cost model. That's an important part of the market, but that can never put guest safety at risk," he said.

He said he wants the investors in the chain to release capital and fund "deep changes" within the company.

Security issues at Travelodge drew the attention of the government early this year. In March, then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security at Travelodge hotels.

An independent review into security at the hotel chain is ongoing and is being led by barrister Paul Greaney KC.

In its statement on Thursday, Travelodge also outlined several measures it was taking to address security issues.

It highlighted a partnership "with a leading Violence Against Women and Girls expert" who is training some of the firm's senior leaders, as well as reviewing the company's existing policies.

Any additional or replacement room keys now require explicit permission from the guest staying in the room, the firm said.

The chain said it had also carried out checks across all of its UK rooms to confirm that all key-card doors have a secondary deadbolt.

Boydell, who stood down on 17 August, has been replaced on an interim basis by the company's chief financial officer Ray Reidy.

In a statement, Reidy said: "We remain focused on the safety and well-being of our guests and will continue taking the actions necessary to strengthen the business.

"We will also continue to engage proactively and constructively with government and the wider hospitality industry on the issue of safety and security."

News.title: School 'deeply saddened' by death of family in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
A school attended by a 14-year-old girl who died alongside her father and mother after getting into difficulty in water off the coast of Shoreham-by-Sea has paid tribute to her.

Sara El-Khawas and her parents Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, are believed to have gone into the water near Shoreham Fort in West Sussex on Tuesday, according to Sussex Police.

In a statement on its website, the Ellen Wilkinson School for Girls in Ealing, west London, described Sara as a "sweet girl, well-liked by staff and students".

A fourth member of the family, a younger girl, remains in hospital in a critical condition.

News.title: Train derailment carriages moved amid track probe
News.content:
Work has begun on removing the carriages of the train that derailed near Lewes with 150 people on board.

Thirty people were injured, two seriously, when the Southern 14:24 BST service from London Victoria to Eastbourne came off the tracks last Thursday.

Video posted on social media, external showed carriages that did not derail being transported through Lewes station overnight, as recovery work continues at the site.

A preliminary report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) found a defect in the track where the train derailed. Network Rail and Greater Thameslink Railway (GTR), which runs Southern, have said they will consider recommendations from the investigation and work to implement them.

Investigators are still examining how the track was inspected and maintained, the condition of the embankment and whether hot weather may have played a role, external.

News.title: Asylum seekers told rape and harassment illegal in UK in new Home Office booklet
News.content:
Asylum seekers have been told that rape, sexual harassment and domestic abuse are illegal in the UK, in guidance for new arrivals published by the Home Office.

A nine-page online booklet covers respect in public, sex and consent, and gender equality, with guidance on how UK laws and customs may be different from their home countries.

The Conservatives said any asylum seekers breaking UK law should be deported and Reform said the publication showed the government "knows that they are a menace".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government had "a very clear principle that if you break UK law, you will be removed from the country".

He said the number of removals of illegal immigrants from the UK "are significantly up" and that he was working to ensure that foreign national offenders are removed from the prison system.

He added: "It follows that if we're taking this approach, it's made explicitly clear what the UK law is and what the societal norms of the UK are and that's why this approach is being taken."

According to the latest Home Office figures, a total of 93,525 people applied for asylum in the UK from April 2025 to March 2026, which was down by 12% on the same period in the previous year.

The booklet sets out how asylum seekers must understand UK law, because the consequences of breaking the law mean "you could get in trouble with the police, lose your asylum support, or it could affect your asylum claim."

A section on gender, external explains that women in the UK have equal rights to men, and do not need the permission from a husband, father, brother or any other man to do things like work, study, travel, or make decisions.

Another section on sex and consent sets out how both people must agree to sex or sexual contact of any kind, and consent cannot be given if someone is asleep, drunk, or unable to respond.

"If you have sex with someone who does not want to, this is called rape. Rape is a serious crime," the document says.

"It is still rape if: You are married to the person or in a relationship. They agreed once, but changed their mind."

News.title: US national debt passes $40tn after doubling in a decade
News.content:
US national debt has more than doubled in a decade to reach a milestone $40tn (Â£29.4tn), Treasury figures show.

The rise reflects years of heavy spending under both the Trump and Biden administrations, along with higher interest payments that have steadily added to the total. In 2016, the national debt stood at just under $20tn.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) had projected overall borrowing would reach $39.6tn by the end of fiscal year 2026, external.

The faster-than-expected rise has sharpened concerns about how quickly the government's borrowing needs are growing and what that means for future interest costs.

The CBO said the US was nearing its $41.1tn debt ceiling, with debt projected to climb to about $64tn by 2036.

As the federal government spends more to cover its budget deficits, consumers have faced higher interest rates and inflation.

The $40.05tn, as of 18 August,, external covers all outstanding Treasury bonds, bills and notes, and underscores the scale of US borrowing under two presidents.

News.title: Pensioner had 'largest hoard' of child abuse images to be seized in Scotland
News.content:
A pensioner amassed what is thought to be the largest collection of child sexual abuse material ever seized by police in Scotland, a court has heard.

Alan MacPherson, 83, from Stenhousemuir, was found to have over two million images on various electronic devices after his home was raided in 2025.

More than 805,000 were formally identified as depicting child sexual abuse - much of it of the most serious category - while the overwhelming scale of his collection meant much of material was not examined.

MacPherson, who admitted downloading the material over a 14-year period, was placed on the sex offenders register and remanded in custody at Falkirk Sheriff Court pending pre-sentence reports.

News.title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged
News.content:
A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences.

Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France.

Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK.

The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police.

He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means.

He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October.

Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught.

Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.

News.title: Thunderstorm warnings expire but rain continues to bring risk of floods for UK
News.content:
Heavy showers and thunderstorms will continue to affect large swathes of the UK on Thursday afternoon, bringing the threat of flooding and travel disruption.

A Met Office yellow thunderstorm covering parts of northern England and north Wales expired at 13:00 BST, with focus of heavy downpours shifting southwards across England and Wales.

Drivers are still being warned that wet weather could lead to slippery conditions and flooded roads.

The Environment Agency has issued one flood warning, external for Walverdon Water in Nelson, Lancashire.

Temperatures are also dropping with some places expected to remain below the August average over the next few days.

News.title: Vapes could lead to health harms in children, doctors warn
News.content:
Vaping could lead to health harms in children and young people and should be made "less attractive" to them, doctors have said.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has reviewed about 81 studies into vaping and said it is linked to higher rates of breathing problems and evidence of harm in babies whose mothers used vapes while pregnant.

The review said vaping should not be seen as a "harmless part of growing up".

The RCPCH is calling on the UK government to go further in its proposals to place new restrictions around the sale of vapes and suggests limiting the number of flavours that are available.

The review into vapes has been published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. Experts from the college looked at the studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people.

It said vaping had an association with problems including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Co-author of the systematic review, Prof Will Carroll, said the evidence showed "clear links" with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking.

"We must act to make vaping less attractive and accessible to children," he said.

Vice-president for policy of the RCPCH, Dr Mike McKean, added: "Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging."

"We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products."

In July, the government launched a 12-week consultation on the appearance, packaging and display of vapes with the aim of reducing the appeal of the products to children.

As part of the new proposals, packs would need to be plain with strict limits on branding and only simple flavour descriptions like "apple" or "cola" used.

Other restrictions would move vapes out of sight in shops, similar to how cigarettes and tobacco are currently sold.

The 100-day consultation follows the recent passing of the Tobacco and Vapes Act,, external which sets out proposals to create the UK's first smoke-free generation.

Children aged 17 or younger now face a lifelong ban on buying cigarettes, since it will be illegal for shops to sell tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.

Dr McKean said the new act was "an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution".

Prof Carroll said the government needed "to go further and limit the types of flavours available to them as opposed to just their descriptions".

News.title: Burnham announces plans to clean up worst three illegal waste dumps
News.content:
Three of the country's worst illegal dumps are due to be cleaned up using taxpayers' money, the government has announced.

Sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire will be assessed for clearance, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the "toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long".

Fines for waste offences will also rise from Â£300 to Â£5,000 to deter, catch, and punish those who dump illegally, and the Environment Agency will have more powers to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime by those involved.

But opposition parties said illegal dumps were a small part of a much bigger issue with smaller scale fly-tipping and landfill all posing big problems for communities.

Burnham is looking to build on work started by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to tackle waste crime, with an action plan published in March detailing a series of measures - including using drones to map illegal waste sites.

Sir Keir's administration had announced that sites in Wigan, Sheffield and Lancashire would have government clean-ups - alongside Kidlington in Oxfordshire where removal of 20,000 tonnes of waste started in April.

The government said the new sites identified for clearance contain around 22,000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste.

They are: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road in Bradford, West Yorkshire.

West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.

The government said this will give mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.

Speaking on a visit to the waste dump in West Yorkshire, Burnham said: "We've begun a much more networked approach to this, where we're bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me."

The prime minister said the aim was to build intelligence about criminals linked to waste dumps at an earlier stage, to avoid the public being charged for clean-ups.

"We should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays," he added.

A new "waste crime crackdown group", chaired by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together in a bid to dismantle criminal operations.

Eagle said: "We are cleaning up sites, but we are also stopping the cycle, driving faster prevention and disruption, better intelligence, and stronger coordination across the system."

News.title: John Swinney defends £45,000 business-class flights to World Cup
News.content:
John Swinney has defended the use of more than Â£45,000 of public funds on business-class flights for him and two senior aides to the World Cup.

The first minister flew to Boston on 11 June for Scotland's opening match, before taking part in trade talks in Kentucky three days later.

While he and two senior officials travelled business class, Sports Minister Maree Todd and several other officials went to the US on significantly cheaper economy-class flights.

Swinney insisted the government had sought to "minimise" costs, while Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the business class flights as a means of ensuring ministers "arrive fresh" when they travel overseas.

In total, the government spent Â£98,442 on trips for Swinney, Todd and their officials to the US, including flights, hotels and expenses.

Flights for Swinney and his private secretary John Webster cost Â£17,893 each.

Business-class tickets for the first minister's special adviser Colin McAllister cost Â£9,864.

News.title: Rare Suffragette Christmas card from 1910 found at roadshow
News.content:
A rare Suffragette Christmas card from around 1910 has been discovered at a vintage roadshow.

The card, found in Mold, Flintshire, and which comes from the height of the campaign to win women the vote, was produced to raise funds and awareness for the movement.

Today, surviving examples are "exceptionally scarce", according to antique shop WeBuyVintage, which has valued the item at Â£2,500.

"These weren't simply Christmas cards, they were pieces of political campaigning that helped fund one of the most significant social movements in British history," said Matt Case, an antiques specialist.

Case said that finding an original Suffragette Christmas card was "incredibly exciting".

Because they were intended to be seasonal and disposable, "very few have survived, especially in such good condition", he added.

Sold by organisations such as the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU), they helped finance the campaign while keeping the movement visible during the Christmas season.

Museums, including the London Museum, external, now hold examples in their permanent collections as important artefacts documenting the fight for women's voting rights.

In Wales, Lady Rhondda, born Margaret Haig-Thomas, led a 40-year campaign for women to be allowed to sit in the House of Lords - although she died just before the law she fought for was changed, too late to take her own seat.

News.title: Weekly type 2 diabetes jab could replace daily injections
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people with type 2 diabetes could get access to a new weekly insulin jab to replace daily injections, reducing the number needed each year by 86%.

Patients still have to wait for the treatment to be approved by the medicines regulator before it is made available on the NHS.

The treatment is said to work as well as daily insulin jabs but only needs to be injected once a week.

The charity Diabetes UK says it will help people manage their condition better, especially those who have extra care needs and who require help to inject every day.

Around 4.7 million people in the UK were living with diabetes in 2024-25, of which roughly 90% had type 2.

The condition means the body can't make enough of a hormone called insulin, or the insulin it makes doesn't work properly - also known as insulin resistance.

Diabetes UK says that around 1 in 4 people with type 2 diabetes takes insulin.

News.title: Farm defends Titanic-themed ride after backlash
News.content:
The owners of a Titanic-themed ride have defended it after criticism it disrespected those who died in the 1912 disaster.

More than 1,500 people drowned when the ship struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic while on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York.

The Titanic ride at Graveley Fruit Farm near Hitchin, Hertfordshire, sees the replica ship lift at one end to slide customers downwards, resembling the sinking of the ocean liner.

Manager Will Campbell-Gray said: "We're keeping the memory of Titanic alive and we're not making fun of the dead at all."

More from Beds, Herts and Bucks:

He added the ride was renamed The Big Tipper last year after complaints were made online, but the original name was restored after his wife received threats demanding it was changed back.

The Titanic was 269m (882ft) long, 28m (91ft) wide and more than 53m (173ft) tall, and took about three years to build.

Its construction cost Â£1.5m, which is about Â£170m in today's money.

News.title: Andy Burnham defends Home Office booklet urging asylum seekers not to rape women
News.content:

Andy Burnham has defended advice handed to asylum-seekers by the government, telling them rape and domestic abuse are serious crimes.

The guidance forms part of a Home Office document entitled “Understanding behaviours and expectations in the UK” which also provides guidance on gender equality and respect in public.

The nine-page document published on Wednesday says it is to help “understand what is expected of you when living in the UK” and the “rules and expectations are not just for people seeking asylum, they apply to everyone living here”.

It advises that rape, sex with someone under the age of 16 and domestic abuse are “serious crimes” which could lead to prison and loss of support and accommodation, as well as affecting asylum claims.

The prime minister defended the advice, telling reporters on a visit to an illegal waste dump in Bradford, West Yorkshire that he has “made explicitly clear what the UK law is and what the societal norms of the UK are”.

open image in gallery The guide spells out that anyone breaking the law could lose their asylum support ( Home Office / gov.uk )

“As a government, we have a very clear principle: if you break UK law, you will be removed from the country and we have seen that in relation to immigration, where removals are significantly up,” he said.

“I’m currently working to ensure that foreign national offenders who can be removed from the prison system are removed from that system.

“So it follows that if we’re taking this approach, it’s made explicitly clear what the UK law is and what the societal norms of the UK are, and that’s why this approach is being taken.”

School standards minister Georgia Gould said that the starting point of asylum seekers coming to this country is "understanding the laws of this country”, but warned against making “full generalisations”.

open image in gallery The prime minister defended the approach on a visit to West Yorkshire on Thursday ( PA )

Asked about whether there are concerns about some migrants coming from other countries, she said the treatment of women in countries such as Afghanistan was “obviously very, very different and deeply concerning”.

“But it is for many people who come from Afghanistan,” she told Times Radio. “And when I used to lead Camden Council, we had a really large number of Afghan evacuees who came into Camden, and I spent many, many hours with those families. These are people who served alongside British troops who were, you know, acted as security families.

“And these were, you know, wonderful people who wanted to contribute, who had, you know, done a huge amount in their country and had a huge amount that they wanted to contribute to our country.”

In response to presenter Stig Abell saying there are some men “come from a culture which doesn't value women”, she said: “I don't think it's possible to make those kind of full generalisations.

“My experience of having worked very closely with Afghan refugees, is that, you know, that there is, you know, very many people who were so proud to be in a country that supported women.”

The booklet explains that women have equality in Britain and are free to work, study, travel and make decisions about their lives, and says anyone not following the rules may be in trouble with police or lose their accommodation and support and could have their asylum claim rejected.

open image in gallery Migrants are warned against following people and making rude gestures ( Home Office / gov.uk )

The nine-page Home Office guidelines also includes phone numbers and links to sites where migrants can get help.

In the section entitled “sex and consent”, the guidance tells asylum seekers that “consent is needed in every situation”.

The guidance also covers gender equality, saying equal rights are “an important part of UK culture… protected by law”.

It also calls for respect for others “even if you disagree with their beliefs or how they live” and provides helplines for those affected by abuse.

Asylum-seekers are also warned not to make sexual comments, even if they think it is a compliment; whistle or make kissing noises at someone; follow someone or block their path or make rude or offensive gestures.

A separate leaflet published at the same time, called Keeping Children Safe in the UK, warns that female genital mutilation and forcing a child to marry are serious crimes in the UK.

The government says it wants no possible misunderstanding of what is expected of asylum-seekers.

open image in gallery More than 93,000 people claimed asylum in the UK in the year to March ( AFP/Getty )

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We expect everyone who comes to the UK to abide by our laws. If they do not, they will face consequences, including the refusal of their asylum claim and removal from the UK.

“Returns of failed asylum-seekers have reached their highest level since 2010 under this government.”

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: “It seems like every day there is another report of an illegal immigrant raping or assaulting women and young girls here. Instead of trying to train these mainly young, male illegal immigrants to behave in a civilised way towards women, the Home Office should instead deport them.”

In a video posted on X, Reform home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf described the guidance as a “disgrace”, which shows the government knows asylum seekers are a “menace”.

Siya Kolisi has been left out of the South Africa side to face New Zealand in the first Test in Johannesburg.

Springboks skipper Kolisi had been battling back from a hamstring injury ahead of the encounter at Ellis Park, and has been overlooked on the openside despite trainning this week.

Paul de Villiers is preferred in the back row as Pieter-Steph du Toit again captains Rassie Erasmus’s side.

Ox Nche is fit to start at loosehead prop, while Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu gets the nod ahead of Handre Pollard and Manie Libbok at fly half.

Centre Damian de Allende earns his 100th cap in an experienced midfield with Jesse Kriel, while Andre Esterhuizen provides both backline and back row cover from the bench.

“Siya trained well with us this week, and although we could have selected him for this clash, we thought it would be best to select Paul (de Villiers) for this weekend’s game,” head coach Erasmus explained.

“We are playing four Tests against the All Blacks and Paul has been playing well, so we are excited to give him a chance this weekend in what will be his first Test match against New Zealand, while taking a precautionary approach to Siya’s return.”

Kolisi missed all three of the world champions’ Nations Championship fixtures in July with injury, before suffering a fresh hamstring issue in the game against Argentina earlier this month.

The meeting in Johannesburg is the first of four Tests between the Springboks and All Blacks that form the centrepiece of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour, which concludes with a match in Baltimore on 12 September.

South Africa XV to face New Zealand (Saturday 22 August, 4.10pm BST): 1 Ox Nche, 2 Malcolm Marx, 3 Wilco Louw; 4 Eben Etzebeth, 5 Ruan Nortje; 6 Paul de Villiers, 7 Pieter-Steph du Toit (capt.), 8 Jasper Wiese; 9 Grant Williams, 10 Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu; 11 Kurt-Lee Arendse, 12 Damian de Allende, 13 Jesse Kriel, 14 Cheslin Kolbe; 15 Damian Willemse.

Replacements: 16 Jan-Hendrik Wessels, 17 Gehard Steenekamp, 18 Zachary Porthen, 19 Cobus Wiese, 20 Andre Esterhuizen, 21 Marco van Staden; 22 Cobus Reinach, 23 Manie Libbok.

News.title: Tinder conman claimed he had cancer in devious trap to swindle victims out of £70k
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Joseph Gibson claimed he had cancer, said he had been blown up by a bomb and even claimed to be worth more than £440m – but his devious pack of lies were all part of a trap to swindle his victims out of almost £70,000 and uphold the illusion of a luxurious lifestyle.

Two of his victims, who he met on Tinder, were taken in by his ploy, handing over money they believed would fund private cancer treatment and clothes. One woman, who believed she was in a relationship with him, took out personal loans and built up credit card debts as she lost more than £21,000.

So sophisticated and drawn-out was the 35-year-old silver-tongued lothario’s fraudulent scheme, that he sent photographs of himself in a hospital bed and begged for money.

Meanwhile, he told another victim he was a multi-millionaire and encouraged them to hand over cash they thought they were investing in his business.

open image in gallery Joseph Gibson was sentenced for fraud at Bristol Crown Court on Thursday ( Avon and somerset Police )

Gibson, of Penbryn Nant, Ruthin Wells, was sentenced to three years and two months in prison at Bristol Crown Court on Thursday after earlier pleaded guilty to four charges of fraud, relating to three women and one man, who he conned out of £68,000 between July 2020 and October 2021. The figure was originally estimated by the police to be around £80,000.

Pictures and text messages sent by the fraudster to his victims, released by Avon and Somerset Police, illustrate the extent of his cruel offending.

Two images showed Gibson in a hospital bed with a face mask, another showed a blood catheter in his wrist, which also bore a hospital band.

open image in gallery Joseph Gibson sent a picture of himself 'in hospital' as he asked one victim for cash ( Avon and Somerset Police )

open image in gallery Gibson even sent a picture of a blood catheter in his wrist ( Avon and Somerset Police )

In a text message to one of his victims, he wrote: “I think the cancer is back x”. Later, he continued: “See the DR, it’s cancer and he wants to start radio Tuesday. Do not tell anyone please x. Yeah, it is deffo cancer.”

On another occassion, while claiming to be in hospital, he texted a victim “very embarrassed”, asking them to buy him clothing. “Nothing design haha and have to delivered to the hospital and I’ll pay you when out if can’t I understand but can’t ask anyone else,” wrote.

After she asked for his spending limit, he replied that he was valued at £440m.

open image in gallery Text message to victim asking for clothing to be sent to the hospital he said he was at ( Avon and Somerset Police )

open image in gallery He then tells a victim that he is valued at £440m after asking for clothes while in hospital ( Avon and Somerset Police )

Gibson had repeatedly told his victims he had cancer, Ellen Macanaw, prosecuting, told an earlier hearing. His first victim, a Devon-based businesswoman he met on Tinder, sent him £100 after he told her he had the disease, and that “he had people on his back again for money”, the court heard.

The victim then received the pictures of him purporting to be in hospital as he asked for more money, leaving the woman, who lost more than £5,200 over a four-month period, with just 93p in her bank account. Ms MacAnaw said he had plied her with lies, claiming to be worth more than £400m, in charge of many businesses and owning yachts.

She handed him most of her cash, believing he was using it to purchase stock for her retail business.

“It really upsets me when I hear about people having cancer because I question whether they are telling me the truth,” she said in her victim impact statement after he was caught.

open image in gallery Gibson tells one victim he has a military degree in neurological biological chemical welfare ( Avon and Somerset Police )

Gibson told his second victim, who he also matched with on Tinder, that he was at University College London Hospital receiving treatment for radiation damage suffered while in the Royal Navy, while also claiming to have been “blown up by an IED,” Ms MacAnaw said.

Telling her he could invest her money while making her believe they were in a relationship, he told her his cancer had returned and he needed money urgently for private treatment. The victim took out a £4,000 loan to help him pay for it.

Like with his first victim, he made up stories of his wealth, telling her he was thinking of buying a yacht in Corfu for around £6m.

open image in gallery The picture of the yacht Gibson told one victim he was considering buying ( Avon and Somerset Police )

The woman took out personal loans and built up credit card debt as a result of the con, losing more than £21,000. “He has broken me as a person and turned my whole world upside down”, she said in her victim impact statement.

Two other victims were targeted by Gibson’s fabricated lies.

open image in gallery Gibson pleaded guilty to four charges of fraud by false representation, which occurred between July 2020 and October 2021 ( Rod Minchin/PA Wire )

A third, who was a relative of the second victim, took out loans to invest in bogus investment deals pushed by Gibson. In total she lost over £18,000.

The fourth was a former captain of a super yacht who had been taken in by the fraudster’s lies about his interest in sailing and boats. He gave Gibson more than £25,000 to invest in his business.

The man said in his victim impact statement: “Joe is a psychopathic con artist who would not stop taking money from people. He is a danger to society.”

In the released text messages on Thursday, Gibson told one victim he had climbed Everest. He told one he had a boat “to do Europe for long weekends” and a flat in Dubai, as he asked for £20 to buy deodorant and shampoo during a flight.

In another message he told a victim “Sandbanks is my retreat to get away from hustle and bustle”, adding he had a house and 21 rented properties along the affluent neighbourhood in Poole, Dorset.

He also told a victim he had a “beautiful place in Mayfair”. He also bragged that he could fly a helicopter and that he had a new yacht in Monaco.

King Charles was informed of plans for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle to move back to the UK only three days ago, it’s been revealed.

The Duke and Duchess are understood to be moving back to the UK later this month in a shock development six years after they relocated to the US. The couple are expected to make their home in a non-royal residence outside London and have already enrolled Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet in British schools.

Charles, who is living with cancer, was first made aware of the move on Sunday, three days before the news was made public, but he is understood to welcome the opportunity to see more of the family.

It is understood there will be no change to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s role and status as private individuals and non-working members of the royal family, and they will not be offered a “half-in-half-out” option when it comes to these roles.

Their security arrangement has been described by the prime minister as a “private matter”.

Andy Burnham said: "It's a matter for Harry and Meghan and we wish them well in the move that they’re making."

Wolverhampton Wanderers have confirmed that they will not play a controversial song in the build-up to kick off for games at the Molineux this season.

The Liquidator song was originally banned several years ago due to its offensive chants aimed at bitter Black Country rivals West Brom and the club held a review to determine if it should be brought back.

Discussion were held with the Molineux Stadium Safety Advisory Group (SAG), which includes representatives from relevant statutory agencies and key stakeholders, as well as supporters before coming to their decision.

An update issued by the Championship club on Thursday announced the decision to stop playing the song before matches in a statement which reads: “Having considered the history of the song, the views expressed by supporters and the club’s responsibilities around supporter behaviour, safety and governance, Wolves has decided that The Liquidator will not be reintroduced into the pre-match entertainment schedule at Molineux.

“The club recognises the significance of the song to sections of the Wolves support and its long association with the atmosphere at Molineux, however football, and the regulatory environment in which clubs operate, have changed considerably over the past two decades.

“In recent seasons, Wolves has been sanctioned by the Football Association in relation to mass discriminatory chanting, and against that backdrop, the club does not believe it would be appropriate to reintroduce a song which has historically prompted mass offensive chanting at Molineux.”

Wolves executive chairman Nathan Shi added: “When I spoke to supporters in May, I said we would look at this issue again properly, and we have done that.

“We have considered the different views, reviewed the history and context, and consulted with the Safety Advisory Group. Having gone through that process, we believe this is the right decision for the club.

“I respect what The Liquidator means to many Wolves supporters and its place in the history of Molineux, but we also have a responsibility to make decisions based on where the club is today and the standards we expect around our matchday environment.”

Georgia senator Jon Ossoff has said it is “amazing to watch this White House melt down” over his comments about President Donald Trump’s executive assistant Natalie Harp.

At a re-election rally at the weekend, the Democratic rising star said of Trump: “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job; he wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie to their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

He was referring to the new Air Force One plane, which was donated by the Qatari government last year as an “unconditional gift”.

open image in gallery Jon Ossoff ‘s remarks on Natalie Harp and Trump went viral and prompted a fierce response from the White House ( Getty )

Harp, 35, is one of Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides. She is reportedly trusted with typing out his Truth Social posts, among other responsibilities.

His remark went viral and prompted a fierce response from the White House, with Communications Director Steven Cheung posting on X: “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics.”

He continued: “Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he's a miserable person who hates this country. It's because he's a radical, extremist Dumocrat.”

Other MAGA allies also attacked Ossoff. White House spokesman Davis Ingle posted: “Jon Ossoff is a cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama. Nobody gives a shit what this lightweight loser says.”

On Monday afternoon Trump dismissed a CNN reporter who asked him about Ossoff’s remarks, instead referring to the senator as “Pee-Wee Herman,” a 1980s comedic character.

open image in gallery Natalie Harp, the president's executive assistant, is one of Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides ( AFP via Getty Images )

The feud escalated on Tuesday, when Ossoff called Trump “a draft-dodging, crook president who has plunged our nation recklessly into a war he knows not how to end or to win.”

On Wednesday’s The Last Word on MS Now, host Laurence O’Donnell aired the clip and asked Ossoff about the comments.

“Senator, of all the things you’ve said about Donald Trump – and there are many – this is the one that apparently bothers him and everyone at his White House the most,” O’Donnell said.

Ossoff responded: “It’s been amazing to watch this White House melt down over this all week.”

Referring to Natalie Harp and other staffers, he said: “These White House staffers are adults, public officials paid by the taxpayer with immense power in positions of public trust. And whether it’s Natalie Harp printing out Donald Trump’s daily dose of delusion and flattery, or Peter Navarro steering taxpayer-funded loans to Trump family investments, or Pete Hegseth deluding the president daily into deepening this quagmire in the Middle East, no one cares about their feelings.”

Taiwan 's government on Thursday proposed a record-high defense budget of 1.12 trillion Taiwan dollars ($35 billion) for next year, signaling intensifying efforts to deter China's military threats.

The administration's planned increase in military spending came after China stepped up its military and political pressure in recent years, asserting its claims that Taiwan was part of its sovereignty.

China sends military planes, as well as coast guard ships and other vessels, toward Taiwan regularly and carries out large-scale military exercises from time to time. It has not renounced the use of force to bring the island under its control.

Under Taiwan's plans, the island's defense spending next year will exceed 3% of its estimated gross domestic product. The amount would be an 18% jump from last year's proposed budget, according to a government statement.

The government's overall spending plans, including on defense, will be sent to the opposition-controlled legislature for review before late August, it said. But the process may come with some challenges.

The legislature only passed the central government’s 2026 budget last Friday, after a record 266-day delay, Taiwan's Central News Agency reported.

Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te previously pledged to raise defense spending to 5% of the island’s GDP by 2030. On Monday, Lai said next year's defense budget would go beyond 1 trillion Taiwan dollars for the first time, adding that investing in national defense is an investment in peace.

Earlier this month, the island ramped up the intensity of its annual Han Kuang drills, aimed at modeling a response to a possible Chinese military invasion. It incorporated reservists and more civilians into the exercises with a focus on real-world scenarios. Mobile internet in parts of Taiwan was briefly slowed to text-only speed.

Previously, urban resilience drills in Taipei went largely unnoticed as they were not disruptive.

The United States has demanded that Taiwan raise its defense spending.

Washington does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but maintains extensive unofficial relations and is required under U.S. law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. Under that framework, the U.S. has long been Taiwan’s main informal backer and arms supplier, a relationship that created tensions with Beijing.

When U.S. President Donald Trump visited Beijing in May, China’s President Xi Jinping warned him that their two countries could clash over Taiwan if the issue is not handled properly.

After Trump's trip to Beijing, he said arms sales to Taiwan were a “very good negotiating chip” with China, comments that stirred anxieties on the island.

China and Taiwan have been governed separately since 1949, when a civil war brought the Communist Party to power in Beijing. Defeated Nationalist Party forces fled to Taiwan. The island has operated since then with its own government.

A court on the Indonesian resort island of Bali sentenced a Swiss tourist on Thursday to one year in prison for insulting a sacred Balinese Hindu observance.

Luzian Andrin Zgraggen, 26, was found guilty of violating Indonesia’s new criminal code by posting social media messages about the Day of Silence, when people are required to stay home and are urged to remain silent and meditate.

The Denpasar District Court determined that he posted the messages even after staff at the villa where he was staying informed him of the restrictions.

“What the defendant did offended the Balinese people, hurt their faith and provoked public outrage,” said presiding judge Tjokorda Putra Budi Pastima. “The defendant must be held accountable for his actions.”

The Day of Silence, locally known as Nyepi, usually falls in March. For a day, the island's world-famous beaches and streets are empty of people except for special patrols meant to ensure silence is observed. The airport in Bali, a predominantly Hindu island in Muslim-majority Indonesia, shuts down and the internet is switched off. The restrictions apply to everyone regardless of religion or nationality.

Zgraggen boasted in Instagram posts that he had defied restrictions that prohibit residents and visitors from leaving their homes or accommodations except for emergencies.

In video clips shared online, Zgraggen smiled at the camera and described walking to a beach during the observance. In one, he called the tradition “crazy” and used an expletive.

The posts were widely reposted on social media, triggering condemnation from Balinese residents who considered them disrespectful. Authorities tracked him down following public complaints, and he was arrested at a villa in Legian, a popular tourist spot near Kuta Beach.

During his trial, which began in June, Zgraggen told the court he had never intended to insult the Hindu holiday or the Balinese people. He said he made the posts while hungry and frustrated that he could not obtain food during the shutdown. He said he had not fully understood the extent of the restrictions.

“I deeply regret what I did, I apologize to the Balinese people,” Zgraggen said in his defense plea.

While authorities have previously detained foreign and domestic tourists for venturing outside during Nyepi, those cases were generally resolved without prosecution.

News.title: Robinson demolishes Pakistan to cement importance to new regime
News.content:
He also has that edge, the grunt of an angry fast bowler, and his competitiveness was just what Root needed considering his other quicks were still in Hundred mode. Archer bowled too short, Gus Atkinson grew into the innings but was wicketless and it took a while for Tongue to click, although once he did he was unplayable against the right-handers with his pace and angle.

Robinson’s lack of pace gives them the keeper-standing-up option. It worked a treat when he bowled Pakistan’s top-scorer, Abdullah Shafique for 61, his footwork messed up by Jamie Smith breathing down his neck.

Pakistan would have batted first had they won the toss and it is a good pitch that will improve as the Test goes on, although with rain around all week the overheads will have a say on the game. Pakistan have far more recent red-ball exposure than England’s batsmen but they were ill-equipped to deal with Robinson and Tongue.

Most supporters were still walking into the ground when the former struck first ball, Azan Awais lbw to a nip-backer. Shan Masood’s stilted footwork was ripe for exposing and Robinson’s first ball over the wicket to the left-hander was full and straight to beat the loose drive.

Imam-ul-Haq had done the hard work, seeing off Robinson only to flash a drive to second slip off a wide ball from Tongue to end Pakistan’s only stand of substance of the innings: 93 for the third wicket.

Robinson cracked the innings open further with Saud Shakeel leg before, who was too slow to call for the review that would have saved him. Hawk-Eye showed the ball would have gone over the top.

Robinson then bowled Shafique in his next over and Pakistan were toppling. Tongue cranked up the pace, bowled full and the perpendicular angle into the right-handers did the rest.

News.title: Burnham blames Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation
News.content:
Andy Burnham has blamed Donald Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation in Britain.

Inflation jumped from 2.6pc in June to 2.9pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics, threatening to undermine Mr Burnham’s pledge to bring down the cost of living.

The Prime Minister said: “We can’t control though what is going on in the Middle East and the effect of the conflict there is now being felt in inflation here, and in other countries around the world.

“I realise these times are really hard but already people can see a month into office I have done things that will make a difference.”

July’s inflation figure was affected by a 13.5pc rise in the Ofgem price cap in response to the energy crisis unleashed by the Iran war. It means prices are now rising at their highest rate since March.

The latest figure shows the struggle that Mr Burnham faces to fulfil his promise to bring down living costs.

There are fears that inflation will climb higher in the coming months as the impact of the conflict filters through to the economy.

Speaking at an event in the North East, Mr Burnham added: “I want to lead a cost-of-living Government, and I’ve already taken steps as Prime Minister to show I will help people wherever I can. I can’t do everything, I think people know that.

“We’re in tough times, but where I can do something to make life that little bit better, I will do it.”

Since arriving in No 10, Mr Burnham has made tackling the cost of living a key policy focus.

The Prime Minister announced last month that he would remove VAT from electricity bills from October and reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares from next year.

However, average energy bills are expected to jump by around 4pc from October, according to energy analysts Cornwall Insight, wiping out any potential savings from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

The analysts said Ofgem’s price cap – which limits the average annual energy bill faced by a family home – would rise from £1,663 to £1,729.

Despite concerns about increasing gas and electricity bills, July’s rate of inflation was in line with economists’ expectations.

Money markets now expect policymakers at the Bank of England to hold interest rates at 3.75pc at their next meeting in September.

News.title: Unemployment rate fails to fall for Burnham
News.content:
An expected drop in the unemployment rate has failed to materialise, dealing a setback to Andy Burnham’s hopes of reviving Britain’s ailing economy.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

While the three-month figure was flat, monthly data showed a sharp increase at the end of the period. Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

That marked the highest reading since October 2020 and the biggest monthly jump in 13 years.

Julian Jessop, at the Institute of Economic Affairs, described the latest jobs figures as “dire”.

He said: “The unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, with a big jump in the single month figure for June.”

It came as private sector wage growth slumped to a six-year low of just 2.8pc. That stands in contrast to a 6.1pc pay increase for the average public sector worker in the same period.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, warned that the UK was “trapped in a deepening jobs drought”.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “Stagnant, or even negative, real wage growth in the second half of this year will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living.

“However, doing anything substantial without breaching either the fiscal rules or the manifesto commitments looks increasingly difficult given the deterioration in headroom and commitments to spend big on everything from defence to social care.”

News.title: Top British scientist steps down from WHO
News.content:
One of Britain’s best-known scientists has resigned as assistant director-general of the World Health Organization.

Sir Jeremy Farrar became a household name during the pandemic when he served on the UK’s Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies (Sage).

Sources inside the WHO and the broader scientific community told The Telegraph he resigned his position on Monday.

While it is not clear what prompted his resignation, colleagues told The Telegraph he had been unhappy within the organisation for some time. One speculated that he had become increasingly frustrated with its internal politics and bureaucracy.

Sir Jeremy, 64, who was also a former director of the Wellcome Trust, could not immediately be reached for comment.

The surprise move comes at a difficult time for the WHO, which is undergoing a major restructuring after suffering cuts and a massive funding shortfall following the United States’s withdrawal from it in January. It is also fighting a major outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s Director-General, announced Dr Farrar’s decision in an email to all staff on Tuesday morning, saying that the British scientist will “retire” from the WHO, effective September 30.

In the email, seen by The Telegraph, Dr Tedros said: “Dr Farrar has demonstrated an exceptional commitment to science and public health at the highest levels, and we are grateful that he chose to bring his experience, energy and conviction to WHO.

“On behalf of the entire organisation, I extend my sincere thanks to Dr Farrar... [and wish] him every success in his next chapter and a well-deserved retirement.”

He added that Dr Bruce Aylward will take over as the new Assistant Director-General for Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Care.

Sports.title: Arsenal legend backs Mikel Arteta to match rarely-seen title feat already achieved by Man Utd and Chelsea
Sports.content:
LEE DIXON has backed his former club Arsenal to achieve back-to-back Premier League titles for the first time ever.

And the Gunners legend is convinced that Mikel Arteta’s side hasn’t even hit its peak yet.



Dixon, 62, won the league four times during his 14-year stint at Arsenal, but never managed to achieve consecutive titles.

In fact, only Manchester United, Chelsea and Man City have pulled off back-to-back title successes in the Premier League era.



However, Dixon thinks that could all change this season after Arteta put Arsenal back on top last term.

The retired full-back told SunSport, via BestBettingSites, Dixon said: “I actually do think they can, because I think the biggest thing everybody talks about is how difficult it is to get over the line the first time.



“And that is true, in hindsight. Going back over my time, getting over the line was easier – we got over the line in my first full season at Arsenal. And also Arsene’s first full season in 1998, we won the Double.

“But Arteta has been in a position where the lead-up to winning the league has been so highlighted and drawn out based on their previous results of finishing second every year.

“The build-up has been progressive, and finally they did it last year – and I see this team as not even peaked yet.”

Arsenal finished seven points above second-placed Man City last term as they ended their 22-year wait for a Prem title.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Boss Arteta has already spoken about trying to take the team to a “different dimension this season and knows that means making marquee signings.

Gunners chiefs have already splashed over £100m to bring in Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle and Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge this summer.

For Dixon, the new arrivals make Arsenal’s chance of repeating last season’s success even greater.

He added: “I do believe they’ve got a real opportunity to win back-to-back Premier League titles.



“Obviously, with the signings, Guimaraes is a wonderful signing for Arsenal based on what we needed at times last year.

“You look at the midfield and you go, ‘yeah, Declan Rice is brilliant at what he does, but do we have somebody who can create and set the team up?’

“Yes, with Odegaard, but at times with him being out injured, we’ve struggled in that department.

“I think Guimaraes really fills that gap, so I’m very hopeful and quite optimistic about them going back-to-back.”



Dixon didn’t just win the league while at Arsenal, but was part of both of the Gunners’ 1998 and 2002 double-winning sides.

Arsenal were within touching distance of a treble last season, losing the Carabao Cup final to Manchester City and the Champions League final on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain.

Dixon’s domestic doubles came thanks to success in the Premier League and the FA Cup.

Arsenal crashed out of the FA Cup in the quarter-finals last season, losing 2-1 to Championship side Southampton.



Dixon reckons that a domestic double could still be out of reach for Arsenal this year, suggesting they have a better chance of winning the Premier League again than the FA Cup.

He added: “I think they’ve got a bigger chance of winning the Premier League again than the FA Cup.

“The FA Cup is always a few balls in the air, because even though you’re playing fewer games and it’s theoretically easier to win, you could draw Manchester United in the third round or Liverpool in the fourth.

“It can be really difficult. Because they’ve got over the line in the league, I think they’ve got a really good chance of doing that again.

“The FA Cup still has a bit of luck involved, but the power they’ve got throughout every department suggests they’ll go deep in all the competitions they’re competing in.”

Sam Curran's hopes of a Test comeback have been put on hold as he undergoes surgery on a groin injury.

The Surrey all-rounder had been expected to join England for the ongoing Pakistan series, potentially earning what would have been his first Test appearance since 2021.

But Curran has been booked in for an operation following the conclusion of The Hundred, ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

"Sam Curran has been assessed for a groin injury and will undergo surgery on Friday. He will not be available for the remainder of the home season," a Surrey statement read.

Curran's team-mate Will Jacks has also been ruled out of the Pakistan Test series after having his appendix removed, but Surrey confirmed he was recovering ahead of the white-ball series against Sri Lanka.

"Will Jacks is currently recovering after a successful operation to remove his appendix. We will monitor his recovery and assess his availability ahead of the Sri Lanka series," the Surrey statement concluded.
